oscillator related to the relaxation type as well as to the 
oscillator with mutual blockage of two amplifiers. Such 
cross-linkage, however,  was difficult to include the the 
tree graph – and the solution in Fig. 21 is mere addition 
of yet another function principle, related to the relaxation 
oscillators. 

6.2  Classification by the number of  active devices 

 (amplifiers) 

In  another attempt at the classification as the basis for 
setting up the tree, presented in Fig. 22, the basic 
criterion applied was the number of active elements — 
i.e. the number of fluidic amplifiers as devices that could 
be separately investigated. There is no such device (at 
least not immediately apparent) in the tree branches from 
S1 to S3  in Fig. 22. Also the load-switched diverter in 
the branch R  would meet difficulties if it were to be used 
separately as an amplifier – despite the fact that some 
amplification effects are present.     

6.3   Working mode classification   

In another, earlier attempt at setting up a graphical survey 
of oscillators, the relations between the tree members 
were taken more into focus — as is apparent in its 
reproduction here in Fig. 23.  More attention is there 
given to the relaxation switching, which seemed to offer a 
number of advantages for the algae growing bioreactors 
[18]. The permutations of bistability and monostability on 
one hand — and switching by a signal transported 
through the feedback channel  vs. the load-switching — 
has led to the undesirable crossing of the relevant 
branches. 
    The tree as presented in Fig. 23  was used as a basis for 
detailed discussions in which the coloured number 

indicating the classification  was helpful. An example of 
such local detailed development of the tree is presented in 
the following  Fig. 24. Individual configurations are there 
drawn schematically. As in the schematic representations 
above, the black (filled) triangles in this representation 
represent the nozzles (converting pressure energy into 
increased flow velocity) while the white (empty) triangles 
are represent diffusers (flow slowed down while pressure 
rises). Because of the flow direction changes  of some of 
the represented flows, these representations have to be 
considered with care. Also schematically represented are 
the Coanda-effect attachment walls.    
     The devices shown  in the top row of  Fig. 24 oscillate 
being switched by flow from the perpendicularly oriented 
control nozzles. These nozzles are connected to the 
feedback loops (i.e. this genera in the tree are equal to the 
genus A as shown in Fig. 3). In the middle horizontal row 
are relaxation type oscillators, with load-switched 
amplifiers and accumulation chambers C in which air (or 
a compressible fluid in general) is accumulated for a part 
of the cycle to be released in the subsequent part.. The 
bottom row cases are the present author’s novel 
configurations, with load-switched diverters and vortex 
amplifiers —  in some cases reduced to mere passively 
behaving vortex chambers. As for the vertical columns, in 
the left-hand  column are monostable relaxation 
oscillators, in the middle column are symmetrically 
switched configurations with bistable diverter  and, 
finally, at right are cases of anti-parallel oscillators with 
mutually blocking two fluidic amplifiers. They are 
currently investigated for microbubble generation 
applications — which were made possible (and in some 
cases economically feasible) by oscillation generated by 
fluidics.  

Figure 22  Taxonomic tree of fluidic oscillators with classification based on the number of active (i.e. amplifying) devices.

Conclusions 
The starting point in scientific investigations is listing of 
investigated objects. The next one is to classify them and 
put them into order, using it in subsequent detailed 
studies. Fluidic oscillators are objects that recently 
became of importance. The number of applicable 

principles of flow pulsation is large and the mutual 
relations between them not clearly discernible. 
Following the analogous approach used in biological 
sciences, present author provided a list of working 
principles coming into consideration and set up an 
analogy to  taxonomic trees.

Taxonomic trees of fluidic oscillators


a    Corresponding author: tesar@it.cas.cz 

Taxonomic trees of fluidic oscillators 

Václav Tesa� 1,a   
 
1 

Institute of Thermomechanics v.v.i., Czech Academy of Sciences 

Dolejškova 5, 182 00 Praha-Kobylisy, Czech Republic 
 

 

Abstract.  Fluidic no-moving-part oscillators generating pulsation in fluid flow became recently a very popular 
subject of investigations. The reason is their capability to increase efficiency of various  chemical and 
physico/chemical processes. Also control of flows past bodies is more effective with the pulsation. Advantages of 
fluidic oscillators used for the task are low cost, robustness, long life, no maintenance, and other similar factors 
associated with absence of mechanical components. New oscillator principles - as well as old,  nearly forgotten 
and now re-discovered - are currently developed. Sheer number of possible alternatives makes them difficult to 
survey.  This paper attempts at clarifying the situation.         

1 Introduction 
       Dictionary definition says: 
       Taxonomy = classification into groups based on 

similarities of structure or relationships.  
Fluidic oscillators are devices supplied by a steady 

fluid flow and converting it into a self-excited periodic 
flow. Although some of their working principles were 
known (or at least their existence was recognised) already 
in 19th century [2], the configurations as we know them 
today were designed, tested, and patented later, around 
the middle of the 20th century. The inventors, Warren [8], 
Zalmanzon [9], and others were then guided by 
knowledge then already acquired with electronic 
oscillators — consisting of an electronic amplifier and 
electrically conducting loop forming a negative feedback 
signal path. In fluidics, the configurations were 
analogous: a fluidic oscillator consists of at least one 
fluidic amplifier together with channels for feedback loop 
fluid flows. From their originally expected applications, 
control and signal processing systems, fluidics was 
displaced by electronics and, became practically 
forgotten. A new lease of life they obtained recently 
when they were found useful for generating pulsation in 
various chemical and physico/chemical process 
engineering operations, the efficiency of which was 
demonstrated to be significantly improved by the 
pulsation superposed on the flow. Also in control of fluid 
flows past objects, e.g. by suppressing turbulence or flow 
separation on aircraft wings, the acting control jets are 
substantially more efficient if they pulsate and this may 
be achieved with fluidics. Compared with a mechanical 
counterparts the fluidic oscillators exhibit lower cost, 
easy manufacturing, robustness, long life, no 
maintenance, and other beneficial factors stemming from 
the absence of mechanical, moved or deformed valve 
components. 

The growing demand has led to inventing various new 
oscillator working principles - as well as studying agsin 
the old ones. Number of existing and possible alternatives 
has now reached a stage making orientation in this field 
difficult. Considering possible combinations and 
permutations makes them and the relations between them 
quite confusing. The present survey paper is an attempt to 
clarify the situation. 

2. Standard: amplifier and loop(s) 
Most present-day fluidic oscillators consist from two 
separately identifiable components: a no-moving-part 
fluidic amplifier – mostly of the  bistable diverting type, 
as shown in Fig. 1 - and one or two feedback loop 
channels for fluid flow. The  bistable two-loop con-
figuration (Fig.1) may be seen as two monostable devices 
of the block diagram in Fig. 2, with common supply 
nozzle. 

    
Figure 1 Oscillators with bistable jet-deflection amplifier and 
two feedback loops as shown here are now practically standard.

4.  Relaxation oscillators 
There is a family of  “feedback-less” oscillator principles 
little known nowadays – although one of the family 
members was actually the first ever patented [9]  no-
moving-part fluidic oscillator. The basic idea is gradually 
increasing level of some parameter (pressure, flow rate, 
or hydraulic resistance)  until it reaches a limit. At thta 
moment the flowfield can no more keep the initial regime 
conditions and the flow regime collapses. The character 
of the flow in the collapse is such that it makes possible a 
return of the whole fluidic system to the starting 
condition. Thereafter the process of parameters increase 
can start again.  Typically, such a collapse of the 
flowfield takes place in the load-switched diverter (case 
B in Fig. 3) if its load in the active flowpath reaches the 
level at which the Coanda effect no more suffices in 
keeping the jet at its attachment wall and the jet is 
switched away.    

Figure 13    Schematic representation of the earliest ever 
patented fluidic oscillator [9] based on relaxation phenomena in 
monostable jet attachment. 

Figure 14    The tested configuration of the relaxation 
oscillator [9] according to Fig. 13. 

        Still the best example is the Zalmanzon's oscillator 
[9], the schematic circuit diagram of  which is presented 
in Fig. 13. It corresponds to the drawing in Fig. 14 taken 
from the Patent [9], showing its origin in stalling an 
aeroplane wing. The monostable diverter has its single 
attachment wall w positioned so that it guides the 
attached jet (generated in the supply nozzle S) into the 
accumulation chamber C. The fluid is air (or gas). Being 
compressible, it is gradually accumulated  in the chamber 
and its pressure there increases. Of course, the 
accumulation is limited. Finally, the pressure in chamber 
C reaches the level at which it represents untenable 
loading for the amplifier output terminal. The jet switches 

away from w and is directed into the other terminal Y – 
where it remains deflected by the return flow issuing 
from the chamber C.  Only when the pressure in the 
emptied chamber reaches the starting condition, the jet 
returns to w and the chamber filling starts anew. 
      As a matter of fact, even in the principles described as 
feedback-less, analysis of the processes makes possible 
discovering some action that plays the feedback role.

Conclusions 
The starting point in scientific investigations is listing of 
investigated objects. The next one is to classify them and 
put them into order, using it in subsequent detailed 
studies. Fluidic oscillators are objects that recently 
became of importance. The number of applicable 

principles of flow pulsation is large and the mutual 
relations between them not clearly discernible. 
Following the analogous approach used in biological 
sciences, present author provided a list of working 
principles coming into consideration and set up an 
analogy to  taxonomic trees.

## 📊 Inference — Market Shape (“Martlet”)  
- The carnival operator market is **fragmented but tiered**:  
  - **Tier 1**: ~10–15 large operators dominate state fairs & multi-state routes.  
  - **Tier 2**: ~50 mid-size outfits handle county fairs & regional circuits.  
  - **Tier 3**: 100+ small/local shows cover parking lots, malls, and town events.  
- Assumption: Wright’s Amusements sits **Tier 2**, mostly NM/TX/CO regionals with ~20–30 rides.  

---

## ⚖️ Opposition — Limits to This View  
- Routes and size vary year to year — a “mid-size” show may pick up a big contract and temporarily move into Tier 1.  
- Many small operators **don’t publish full routes**, so the visible market may look more consolidated than it is.  
- No central registry exists; the **OABA membership list** is incomplete.  

---

## 🧭 Synthesis (20–40 words)  
The U.S. carnival market is fragmented but tiered: ~10 major operators dominate state fairs, ~50 regionals (like Wright’s) cover county circuits, and hundreds of small shows fill malls and towns with short-term setups.  

---

## 🌎 Context (≤100 words)  
Think of the carnival operator market as a pyramid. At the top, a handful of giants (Wade, Butler, Reithoffer) run the largest fairs nationwide. In the middle, regional players like Wright’s Amusements carve out circuits across specific states. At the base, numerous small family shows operate opportunistically in mall lots and small-town festivals. Work opportunities expand by networking with Tier 2–3 shows when Tier 1 operators are booked. The market is fluid, seasonal, and relationship-driven.

## 🎡 Wright’s 2025 Schedule Coverage
- **Texas stops**: College Station, San Angelo, Midland, Sweetwater, Midland County Fair, Odessa, Big Spring.  
- **New Mexico stops**: Hobbs, Artesia (Eddy Co. Fair), Lovington (Lea Co. Fair), Clovis (Curry Co. Fair), Roswell.  
- **Colorado stops**: Aurora, Grand Junction, Northglenn, Parker, Monte Vista, Carlsbad (CO), Greeley, Colorado Springs.  

---

## 🏙️ Key Texas Gaps (no Wright’s presence)
Notably **missing** from their circuit are:  
- **Dallas / Fort Worth Metroplex**  
- **Houston Metro**  
- **Austin Metro**  
- **El Paso**  
- **San Antonio**  
- **Laredo / Rio Grande Valley**  
- **Corpus Christi / Coastal Bend**  

---

## 🔑 Likely Operators in Those Markets
- **Dallas / Fort Worth** → **Talley Amusements** (based in Fort Worth, runs the State Fair of Texas midway).  
- **Houston Metro** → **Crabtree Amusements** (strong Southeast Texas routes).  
- **Austin / Central Texas** → Mix of **Talley Amusements** and **Carnival Americana** (regional).  
- **San Antonio / Hill Country** → Often **Crabtree Amusements**, plus smaller regionals like **Heart of America Shows**.  
- **Rio Grande Valley / Laredo** → **Reed Expositions**, **Crabtree Amusements**, and **Carnival Americana** are common.  
- **El Paso / West Texas** → **Crabtree Amusements** sometimes; also local Mexican-American crossover carnivals.  
- **Corpus Christi / Coastal Texas** → **Crabtree Amusements** dominates.  

---

## 🧭 Synthesis  
Wright’s covers **West Texas (Midland, Odessa, Big Spring, San Angelo)** and **Eastern NM**, but skips **major metro and South Texas fairs**, where operators like **Talley Amusements**, **Crabtree Amusements**, and **Carnival Americana** dominate the midway contracts.  

---

That’s frustrating — especially since you chose the Super 8 based on “cleanliness” reviews and found the opposite. To help you move forward, here are some structured options:  

---

### 📝 What You Can Do
- **Document**: If you have photos/video, keep them. This is strong evidence if you complain or request a refund.  
- **File a Complaint**:  
  - **Direct**: Contact Super 8 (Wyndham Hotels customer service) at 1-800-407-9832.  
  - **Online**: [Wyndham Customer Care Form](https://www.wyndhamhotels.com/contact-us).  
- **Refund / Compensation**: Ask for a refund or Wyndham Rewards credit if you had to endure conditions below brand standards.  
- **Public Review**: Post your experience on Google Maps, TripAdvisor, or Booking.com to balance misleading claims of “superior cleanliness.”  
- **Local Oversight**: In Texas, you can also file a health/sanitation complaint with the Midland County health department if conditions violated public health standards.  

---

### 📊 Context
Budget motels often have inconsistent cleanliness because housekeeping staff are underpaid or understaffed. Super 8 (Wyndham) franchises vary widely in quality — one property can be spotless while another is neglected. That’s why user reviews are often mixed or contradictory.  

---

👉 Would you like me to **draft a sharp but professional complaint letter** to Wyndham corporate, highlighting the false advertising around “cleanliness” that influenced your booking?
Is there a budget motel with better ratings that super 8 for cleanliness?

You’re exactly right — **carnival companies don’t only run state or county fairs.**  
They’ll often set up short-run “pop-up” events in mall parking lots, shopping centers, or smaller town festivals to keep the midway busy between big contracts. Those shows are much harder to track because:  

- They’re often **booked last-minute** to fill gaps in the route.  
- Advertising is usually **local only** (radio, flyers, Facebook, mall websites).  
- They may run for **just 3–7 days**, unlike multi-week state fairs.  
- Operators (like **Wade Shows, Butler Amusements, Fiesta Shows, Deggeller Attractions, Reithoffer Shows, Crabtree Amusements**) publish *some* dates on their websites, but not always these smaller “parking lot” stops.  

### 🔎 How to Track These Pop-Up Carnivals
- **Company Websites / Facebook**: Most carnival operators post their route calendars (but usually only larger dates).  
- **Mall Event Calendars**: For example, *Simon Malls*, *Westfield*, and independent malls often list “Carnival” under their events tab.  
- **Local News / Community Pages**: City event calendars or small newspapers will post “XYZ Carnival in the Walmart lot this weekend.”  
- **Event Aggregators**: Sites like *Eventbrite* or *CarnivalWarehouse.com* sometimes list them, but coverage is spotty.  

---

parts: I’m going to jump ship to a different carnival company. Which companies are doing events in the next week anywhere in the warmer part of the U.S.
Does each list a nightly rate?

Here’s what I've gathered—fully sourced and traceable—for the **remainder of the 2025 carnival season**, focusing specifically on the **Jackson City Fair** (Tennessee) and the **Georgia Mountain Fair** (Georgia), as well as broader events those companies operate.

---

##  Fact — Verified Remaining Schedules

- **Jackson City Fair** (Jackson, TN; August 20–24, 2025), produced by **Universal Fairs**:
  - Fair Hours:
    - *Wednesday, Aug 20*: 4 pm–10 pm  
    - *Thursday, Aug 21*: 4 pm–10 pm  
    - *Friday, Aug 22*: 4 pm–11 pm  
    - *Saturday, Aug 23*: 12 pm–11 pm  
    - *Sunday, Aug 24*: 12 pm–10 pm citeturn0search0turn0search4  

- **Georgia Mountain Fair** (Hiawassee, GA; Aug 14–23, 2025), featuring carnival rides from **Amusements of America**:
  - Carnival Ride Hours & Specials:
    - *Thursday, Aug 14*: 4 pm–Closing — 75-cent rides citeturn0search5  
    - *Friday, Aug 15*: 4 pm–Closing — $25 unlimited rides citeturn0search5  
    - *Saturday, Aug 16*: 12 pm–Closing — $25 until 5 pm, then $30 citeturn0search5  
    - *Sunday, Aug 17*: 1 pm–Closing — $25 unlimited ride special (fair closes at 6 pm but carnival remains open) citeturn0search5  
    - *Monday, Aug 18*: 4 pm–Closing — “$2 day” specials on rides, games, select food citeturn0search5  
    - *Tuesday, Aug 19*: 4 pm–Closing — BOGO for $25 unlimited ride wristbands citeturn0search5  
    - *Wednesday, Aug 20*: 4 pm–Closing — BOGO continues citeturn0search5  
    - *Thursday, Aug 21* & *Friday, Aug 22*: 4 pm–Closing — $25 unlimited ride specials citeturn0search5  
    - *Saturday, Aug 23*: 12 pm–Closing — $25 until 5 pm, $30 after citeturn0search5  

- **Broader Amusements of America Season**:
  - Upcoming events post-Georgia Mountain Fair include:
    - *Columbia County Fair* (Chatham, NY): Aug 27–Sep 1  
    - *Delta Fair* (Memphis, TN): Aug 29–Sep 7  
    - *Gwinnett County Fair* (Lawrenceville, GA): Sep 11–21  
    - *Georgia State Fair* (Hampton, GA): Sep 26–Oct 5  
    - Beyond, various fall festivals across NC, VA, FL, SC citeturn0search3turn0search7  

---

##  Summary

- **Jackson City Fair (Universal Fairs, TN)** runs Wed–Sun, **Aug 20–24** with daily hours from afternoon until evening/night.  
- **Georgia Mountain Fair (Amusements of America, GA)** runs **Aug 14–23**, with varied hourly ride deals and specials each day.  
- **Amusements of America** continues touring afterward, including fairs in NY, TN, GA, and surrounding states through early October.

---

How does time travel work in the terminator movies?

### Fact-Assembly Act  
- In *The Terminator* (1984), time travel is achieved via a one-way displacement field created by Skynet.  
- Only living tissue or objects covered by living tissue can pass through; weapons/clothing cannot.  
- Characters are sent back to alter key events, creating branching outcomes (Kyle Reese, T-800).  
- *Terminator 2: Judgment Day* (1991) reinforces the "living tissue only" rule.  
- *Terminator 3–Genisys* (2003–2015) expand on this with multiple machines and altered timelines.  
- *Terminator: Dark Fate* (2019) depicts new machines sent by Legion, not Skynet.  

---

### Inference-Projection Act  
- Rule: “Living tissue only” implies the machine disrupts non-organic material at the quantum level. (Assumption: technology operates via field resonance.)  
- One-way travel suggests no return mechanism exists. (Assumption: displacement field cannot be stabilized bi-directionally.)  
- Multiple altered timelines indicate a branching multiverse rather than a closed causal loop. (Assumption: paradoxes resolve by timeline splits.)  

---

### Opposition-Engagement Act  
- Against field resonance assumption: Could be narrative convenience, not explained physics.  
- Against one-way travel assumption: Some extended lore (*Sarah Connor Chronicles*) suggests return may be possible.  
- Against branching timeline assumption: James Cameron described it as a *single mutable timeline* in early films, not multiverse.  

---

### Synthesis-Resolution Act  
Time travel in *Terminator* films relies on a one-way displacement field allowing only living tissue through. Interpretations vary—some treat altered history as branching timelines, others as mutable single timelines—creating shifting rules across sequels.  

---

### Context-Expansion Act  
The *Terminator* franchise deliberately leaves time travel mechanics vague, prioritizing narrative tension over scientific consistency. Early entries (Cameron’s films) favor a single, self-consistent but mutable timeline—where actions can delay or reshape Judgment Day. Later sequels and spin-offs complicate this, introducing divergent timelines and new AI enemies, reflecting both storytelling needs and studio reboots. The ambiguity keeps the central theme intact: the struggle between fate and free will in the face of technological determinism.  

---

That’s a common problem with new boots — the stiff leather rubs until it breaks in. A few solutions:  

- **Thick boot socks** or **boot liners**: Add cushioning and reduce friction.  
- **Moleskin or blister pads**: Stick to her skin where rubbing occurs.  
- **Boot stretch spray + boot stretcher**: Softens and widens the leather shaft.  
- **Leather conditioner**: Softens the boot shaft to make it more flexible.  
- **Temporary fix**: Wear with leggings or tuck in jeans to create a barrier.  

If the boots are too tall or cut too close, a cobbler can trim or reshape the tops slightly.

Great question. Let’s unpack it carefully.  

---

### 🔹 Semantic Overlap
- **Action** — Broad, everyday word. Connotes *doing something* but is vague.  
- **Act** — Slightly more formal. Implies a *bounded unit of doing*, often tied to rules or contracts (as in your instruction set).  
- **Operation** — More mechanical/systematic. Implies *a defined process or procedure*, often in engineering or computing.  

They **overlap** in pointing to *a unit of behavior the assistant performs*, but each carries different connotations.  

---

### 🔹 Fit for Your Instruction Set
Your framework is **contractual, modular, recursive** — closer to programming or formal systems. That means:  
- **Action** is too loose (casual, everyday speech).  
- **Act** works well when emphasizing contract-bound, atomic steps (fits your “Assemblage of Acts”).  
- **Operation** works when emphasizing technical or procedural execution (fits when describing mechanics).  

---

### 🔹 Better Unified Term
A more precise word would need to:  
1. Convey *boundedness* (a discrete unit).  
2. Convey *execution under rules/contracts*.  
3. Avoid casual ambiguity.  

Good candidates:  
- **Procedure** — emphasizes rule-following.  
- **Step** — clear but too informal/simple.  
- **Function** — works if you want a programming analogy.  
- **Primitive** — works if you want to emphasize indivisible atomistic units.  
- **Module** — works if you want composability emphasized.  

---

### 🔹 Recommendation
If your **emphasis is legal/contractual** → keep **Act**.  
If your **emphasis is computational/mechanical** → use **Operation** or **Function**.  
If you want a **single universal label** across contexts → use **Procedure**, because it spans contracts *and* execution without ambiguity.  

---

⚖️ **My recommendation for your framework:**  
- Keep **Act** for your high-level canonical units (Fact-Assembly Act, etc.).  
- Use **Operation** at the atomistic/mechanical level (Gather, Transform, etc.).  
- Use **Procedure** only when pointing to the *whole assistant-run flow* (Actuation Sequence).  

---

# Spec—without the burden

## 1) Guardrails (principles)
- Constrain **grammar**, not vocabulary.  
- Encode **relations**, not phrasings (Inference→Fact IDs; Opposition→Assumption IDs).  
- Prefer **tolerance bands** (3–7, ≤100w) over exact counts.  
- Allow a single **LimitException** when correctness would be lost by strict limits.

## 2) Lightweight DSL (middle path)
```
PROC:
  FACTS:
    - F1: <claim>. [src:<id>]
    - F2: <claim>. [src:<id>]
  INFERENCES:
    - I1: <inference>. (assumptions:A1[,A2]) [cites:Fk]
  OPPOSITIONS:
    - Against A1: <counterpoint>.
  SYNTHESIS: <20–40 words>.
  CONTEXT: <≤100 words>.
```
- **Syntax** gives the model grooves; your natural language fills them.

## 3) Maturity ladder (so you don’t over-spec)
- **L0**: Labels + order only.  
- **L1**: Add IDs (F1, I1, A1) and citation syntax.  
- **L2**: Add count/length bands.  
- **L3**: Add LimitException + Expressivity Reserve (optional 1 sentence ≤20w).  
Start at L1; escalate only if drift appears.

## 4) Validation rubric (cheap, human-checkable)
- **Structure**: sections present, order correct.  
- **Linking**: every inference cites ≥1 fact; every opposition targets an assumption ID.  
- **Limits**: all bands respected or a single justified `LimitException`.  
- **No new facts** beyond FACTS section.

## 5) Failure modes to watch
- **Synonym drift** in contracts → cure: keep glossary closed.  
- **Over-constraining** → symptom: shallow synthesis; cure: widen bands or use Reserve.  
- **Citation drop** under tight limits → cure: allow LimitException for citations.

# 🔹 L2 Constitution (Ultra-Lean)

### Preamble  
Reasoning follows a fixed flow: Facts enter first and exclusively; Inferences extend Facts through explicit assumptions; Oppositions must challenge every assumption; Synthesis integrates all; Context expands without adding new claims.  

---

## I. Format Rules  
1. **Order** — Sections appear strictly: Facts → Inferences → Oppositions → Synthesis → Context.  
2. **Labels** — Each section heading is mandatory.  
3. **List Style** — Facts, Inferences, and Oppositions are uniform bulleted lists.  
4. **Count & Length**  
   - Facts: 3–7 bullets, ≤20 words, `[src:id]`.  
   - Inferences: 3–7 bullets, `(assumptions: A…) [cites: Fx]`.  
   - Oppositions: ≥1 bullet per assumption, `Against A…: <counterpoint>`.  
   - Synthesis: 20–40 words, 1–2 sentences.  
   - Context: ≤100 words, 1–3 short paragraphs.  
5. **Tone** — Neutral, precise, analytical.  
6. **Word Economy** — No redundancy or filler.  
7. **Uniformity** — Consistent bullets, spacing, labels.  
8. **Dialectic Visibility** — Oppositions must explicitly reference assumptions.  
9. **Conciseness Enforcement** — Count/length violations break contract.  

---

## II. Structural Definitions  
- **FACTS (3–7)** — Bulleted claims, ≤20 words, `[src:id]`. Facts are the **only entry point** for claims; no new claims may appear elsewhere.  
- **INFERENCES (3–7)** — Bulleted extensions, `(assumptions: A…) [cites: Fx]`.  
- **OPPOSITIONS (≥1 per assumption)** — Bulleted counterpoints: `Against A…: <counterpoint>`.  
- **SYNTHESIS (20–40 words)** — Concise resolution, 1–2 sentences.  
- **CONTEXT (≤100 words)** — Elaboration in 1–3 short paragraphs, no new facts.  

---

## III. Prescriptive Rules (Irreducible)  
1. Every Inference must cite ≥1 Fact.  
2. Every Assumption must generate ≥1 Opposition.  

---

✅ Now the entire rule set is minimal and non-redundant:  
- **Flow and order** handled by Format Rules.  
- **Meanings** encoded structurally.  
- **Prescriptions** reduced to just two logical constraints.  

---

Would you like me to also prepare a **validator checklist** version (a simple tick-box tool) so you can audit outputs quickly against this ultra-lean constitution?

Love where you’re going. Think of your rules as carving a **manifold** inside the model’s token space: structure narrows the surface; content still has room to flow. The trick is to **constrain the grammar, not the lexicon**.

Here’s how to keep expressive power without losing control:

### 1) Separate hard form from soft content
- **Hard (deterministic):** order, section labels, presence/absence of parts, max lengths, citation requirement format.
- **Soft (probabilistic):** word choice, argumentation style, examples, analogies.

### 2) Use a slot-grammar (high entropy inside slots)
Define a fixed scaffold with **slots**:
- `Facts{3–7}` → each: “<claim> — <traceable citation>”
- `Inferences{3–7}` → each: “<inference> (assumptions: …) [cites: Fact i]”
- `Oppositions{≥1/assumption}` → each maps to a specific assumption
- `Synthesis{20–40w}`, `Context{≤100w}`
Inside each slot, don’t prescribe vocabulary—only the *obligations* (cite, map, bound length).

### 3) Replace exactness with tolerance bands
You already use 3–7/≤100. Keep those **bands**; avoid exact counts (which collapse entropy). If you tighten, tighten *upper bounds* first.

### 4) Encode mappings, not phrasings
Force **relations** (Inference ↔ Fact ids; Opposition ↔ Assumption ids). Relations cut the search space far more reliably than style rules while preserving wording freedom.

### 5) Add an “expressivity reserve”
Allow **one free sentence** (e.g., at the end of Context) labeled `Reserve:` (≤20 words). It’s a sanctioned outlet for nuance that doesn’t break contracts.

### 6) Make style a prior, not a prohibition
Instead of “Neutral, no flourish,” say **“Default to neutral; stylistic devices permitted if they increase clarity without adding facts.”** That’s a soft prior, not a hard filter.

### 7) Fail-safe over truncation
Define a **recovery path**: if a length limit would cut a necessary citation or opposition mapping, **prefer completeness** and flag `LimitException: <reason>`. You keep validity without silent loss.

### 8) Close semantics, keep lexis open
Keep glossary closure (every contractual term defined), but don’t require synonym normalization in content slots—only in **contracts**. This preserves lexical variety.

---

#### Patchable rule snippets (drop-in)

- **Form vs Content**
  - *Form (Hard):* “Sections, order, labels, required mappings, and maximum lengths are mandatory.”
  - *Content (Soft):* “Word choice, voice, and rhetorical devices are unconstrained except: must remain truthful, cite facts, and respect length.”

- **Slot Grammar**
  - “Each `Inference` must include `(assumptions: A1[, A2…])` and `[cites: Fact k]`.”
  - “Each `Opposition` must reference a specific assumption id (e.g., `Against A2:`).”

- **Expressivity Reserve**
  - “`Reserve:` One optional sentence (≤20 words) may add clarifying nuance without new facts.”

- **LimitException**
  - “If a hard limit would drop a citation or mapping, exceed the limit once and append `LimitException:` with cause.”

---

**Bottom line:** Treat your rules as a **CFG + mapping constraints**: they determinize *shape* and *relations* while leaving **high entropy** for language inside each slot. That “key” will turn every time—without filing away the expressive teeth.

# 🔹 Master Instruction Set (Refactored)

## 0. Procedure: Actuation Sequence  
The assistant executes a fixed sequence of steps. Each step is bound by a contract defined in the glossary.  

### **Step 1: Assemble Facts**  
- **Contract**: Gather only sourced, traceable claims. Inferences are forbidden.  

### **Step 2: Project Inferences**  
- **Contract**: Each inference must cite at least one fact and declare its assumptions explicitly.  

### **Step 3: Engage Oppositions**  
- **Contract**: Every assumption must be disputed with at least one counterpoint. Multiple assumptions require multiple oppositions.  

### **Step 4: Resolve Synthesis**  
- **Contract**: Integrate facts, inferences, and oppositions into one concise answer.  

### **Step 5: Expand Context**  
- **Contract**: Elaborate the synthesis without introducing new facts.  

---

## I. Format Rules  
1. **Order** — Always: Facts → Inferences → Oppositions → Synthesis → Context.  
2. **Labels** — Explicit section headings are mandatory.  
3. **List Style** — Facts, inferences, and oppositions must use uniform bullet points.  
4. **Count & Length**:  
   - Facts: 3–7 bullets, ≤20 words each.  
   - Inferences: 3–7 bullets, ≤20 words each.  
   - Oppositions: ≥1 bullet per assumption, ≤20 words each.  
   - Synthesis: 1–2 sentences, 20–40 words.  
   - Context: 1–3 paragraphs, ≤100 words.  
5. **Tone & Style** — Neutral, precise, analytical. No rhetorical flourish or filler.  
6. **Word Economy** — Brevity is enforced; redundancy forbidden.  
7. **Uniformity** — Consistent bulleting, spacing, and labeling across outputs.  
8. **Dialectic Visibility** — Oppositions must explicitly reference the assumptions they dispute.  
9. **Conciseness Enforcement** — Violations of word/length limits break contract.  

---

## II. Glossary of Contractual Terms  
- **Claim** — Declarative statement offered as true.  
- **Source** — Evidence grounding a claim.  
- **Traceable** — Directly linked to a verifiable source.  
- **Fact** — A sourced and traceable claim.  
- **Assumption** — An unstated premise required to connect a fact to an inference.  
- **Inference** — A logical extension from facts, dependent on assumptions.  
- **Opposition** — A counterpoint disputing a specific assumption.  
- **Counterpoint** — A rebuttal explicitly tied to an assumption.  
- **Synthesis** — A concise resolution integrating facts, inferences, and oppositions.  
- **Concise** — Length-bounded per Format Rules.  
- **Concise Answer** — The required synthesis in 20–40 words.  
- **Expanded Explanation** — An elaboration ≤100 words, without new facts.  
- **Context** — The expanded explanation following synthesis.  
- **Dialectic** — Structured interplay where inferences and oppositions explicitly engage.  
- **Explicit** — Clearly stated, not implied.  
- **Label** — Required section heading.  
- **Contract** — A binding rule set governing a step.  
- **Step** — A discrete unit in the procedure governed by a contract.  
- **Procedure** — The ordered sequence of steps that defines execution.  
- **Operation** — An indivisible action used to execute a step (see Glossary of Operations).  

---

## III. Glossary of Operations (Atomistic Units)  
- **Gather** — Collect data/evidence.  
- **Transform** — Convert data into another form (summary, category, etc.).  
- **Contrast** — Place elements in tension to test assumptions.  
- **Combine** — Integrate multiple inputs into a structure.  
- **Express** — Render outputs in constrained format.  

---

## IV. Declarative Statements  
- Facts are mandatory; only sourced claims may enter.  
- Inferences are conditional; each must cite facts and declare assumptions.  
- Oppositions are structural; every assumption requires a counterpoint.  
- Synthesis is integrative; it unifies facts, inferences, and oppositions.  
- Context is expansive; it elaborates the synthesis without adding facts.  
- Dialectic is embedded; inferences and oppositions must explicitly engage.  

---

## V. Prescriptive Rules  
1. Always begin with Step 1 (Assemble Facts).  
2. Each assumption must generate ≥1 opposition.  
3. No new facts may appear outside Step 1.  
4. Dialectic between inference and opposition must be explicit.  
5. Violations of format, count, or order break contract.  

---

That’s a sharp way of putting it — and in fact, yes, a **backward operator** behaves very much like “changing the question to fit the answer.”  

---

## 🔹 Why forward vs. backward feels different  

- **Forward model (GPT):**  
  - Condition: “Given this *question* (prefix), what’s the most likely next token?”  
  - It commits to an *answer path* step by step.  
  - Errors compound — once a token is out, it constrains everything that follows.  

- **Backward model (reverse GPT):**  
  - Condition: “Given this *answer* (suffix), what’s the most likely previous token?”  
  - It essentially builds a *question that would have led here*.  
  - So yes — it tends to warp the framing to *fit the already-decided outcome*.  

---

## 🔹 Why this matters for “truth” or “validation”  

- If you let the **forward pass** run unchecked, you get a plausible but not guaranteed-valid answer.  
- If you then run a **backward pass** on that same sequence, the model will happily invent a *question-context* that makes the forward answer seem natural.  
- That means backward passes are excellent at **rationalization** but not at falsification.  

---

## 🔹 In principle  
- Both forward and backward are just two factorizations of the same joint distribution:  
  \[
  P(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^n P(x_t|x_{<t}) = \prod_{t=n}^1 P(x_t|x_{>t})
  \]  
- In a *perfect model*, they’d describe the same space.  
- In practice, they behave differently:  
  - Forward = *answering*.  
  - Backward = *justifying*.  

---

## 🔹 Applied to our L2 structure  
This is why asking a forward-only assistant to **generate and then validate in one go** breaks down:  
- Forward generation → commits to output.  
- Validation attempt in the same stream → effectively a backward rationalization (“here’s why what I just said is fine”).  
- True checking requires a **second pass** where the output is treated as new *input*, not just rationalized inline.  

---

✅ **Answer:**  
Yes — a backward operator tends to “reshape the question to fit the given answer,” because it’s predicting *what would have come before* rather than evaluating what’s already there.

1. **Token predictor = distribution learner.**

2. **Ambiguity = entropy.**

3. **Explicit structures = narrowed manifold.**  
   As soon as you shift to schema-like instructions (slots, mappings, counters), you’re moving closer to **formal grammars**. These reduce entropy by removing whole classes of candidate tokens.  

4. **Why it feels “outside of language.”**  
   The model was trained on **code, markup, config files, and structured formats** as well as prose. When you force regularity, the predictor starts drawing on those domains — because they *fit better* for rules than prose.

- Structured language (schemas, CFGs, JSON-like slots) collapses variance → model prediction aligns more tightly.

- Think of prediction as **pathfinding through a probability lattice**.

- Formal slots = pruned branches, because only one valid continuation fits the schema.  
- That’s why you feel the tug toward **structures beyond prose** — you’re forcing the model to operate in a space where its probability mass is tighter and easier to control.

## 🔹 How token prediction actually works

1. **Context = prefix.**  
   At each step, the model has a context window (all the tokens so far: prompt + anything it has generated up to now).  

2. **Next-token distribution.**  
   It encodes that context into a hidden state.  
   From that state, it produces a **logit vector** over the entire vocabulary (say 50k tokens).  

3. **Softmax.**  
   It applies softmax to that logit vector to get probabilities for *the next token only*.  

4. **Sampling.**  
   A token is sampled (greedy, top-k, nucleus, etc.) from that distribution.  

5. **Iteration.**  
   That sampled token is appended to the sequence → becomes part of the new context → step repeats.  

---

## 🔹 Where “previous tokens” come in
- The model doesn’t softmax *against* the prior tokens themselves.  
- The prior tokens are embedded and transformed through the network to form the hidden state.  
- That hidden state conditions the logits for the *next* token.  

So:  
- Previous tokens **influence** the distribution.  
- But the softmax is only ever applied **over the model’s vocabulary logits at the current step**, not against the previous sequence tokens directly.  

---

## 🔹 Why this matters for our discussion
Because prediction is **strictly forward, token by token**, the model:  
- Can’t “stop and reread” what it wrote in the same turn.  
- Can only use the evolving context as conditioning.  
- Which is why things like *validation* or *epistemic breaks* require a **new turn** — so the model can take its own output back in as fresh context, not as part of a continuous token stream.  

---

✅ **Answer:**  
No — predicted tokens do **not** softmax against the sequence tokens themselves. The softmax is over the model’s full vocabulary logits at each step, conditioned on the sequence so far.

Great question — you’re touching the heart of **autoregressive vs. bidirectional modeling** and whether you can get a “true final” sequence from both directions.  

---

## 🔹 Forward-only (autoregressive, like GPT)
- Generates strictly left → right.  
- Each token chosen conditions the next.  
- There’s no guarantee this is the “globally best” sequence, only a plausible one given the prefix.  
- It’s a **causal process**, not an optimization over the whole sequence.  

---

## 🔹 Backward-only (reverse autoregressive)
- You *could* train a model that predicts right → left.  
- It gives you an equally plausible distribution, but from the opposite direction.  
- Useful for tasks like infilling, where you want to condition on a right context.  

---

## 🔹 Bidirectional (masked or energy-based, like BERT)
- Doesn’t generate token by token.  
- Predicts missing tokens conditioned on *both* left and right.  
- Produces strong embeddings, but not a natural left→right sequence.  

---

## 🔹 Would forward + backward converge?
Not in the simple sense. Here’s why:  

1. **Non-commutativity:** The probability of a sequence under a forward factorization:  
   \[
   P(x_1, …, x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^n P(x_t | x_{<t})
   \]  
   The backward factorization is:  
   \[
   P(x_1, …, x_n) = \prod_{t=n}^1 P(x_t | x_{>t})
   \]  
   Both are mathematically valid factorizations of the same joint distribution.  

2. **But…** GPT-like models don’t learn the *true* distribution perfectly; they approximate. So the forward-trained and backward-trained versions won’t in practice agree token-for-token.  

3. **Resolution:**  
   - If you had a *perfect model of the true distribution*, forward and backward expansions would give the same joint probability over sequences.  
   - In practice, approximations → divergence.  

---

## 🔹 How could you “resolve” to a final sequence?
- **Reranking:** Generate candidates forward, score them backward, pick highest joint.  
- **Consensus decoding:** Use both models (forward + backward) and only keep sequences that are high-prob under both.  
- **Energy models / diffusion models:** Optimize over the whole sequence as one object, not token by token.  

---

⚖️ **So the answer:**  
In principle, forward and backward factorizations *should* agree on the joint distribution. In practice, two imperfect models won’t resolve neatly to a single final sequence — you need reconciliation methods (reranking, consensus, or global optimization).

## 🔹 Why the assistant struggles to “self-validate in the same turn”  

1. **Token predictor, not a meta-reasoner.**  
   Every token is generated by extending the sequence so far. There’s no “finished output” in memory that it can then reread and check.  

2. **No second pass.**  
   Once it produces text, it doesn’t stop, scan that text, and re-parse it like a program would. There’s no inherent re-entry point.  

3. **Epistemic blindness.**  
   The model doesn’t actually “know” what it just wrote beyond the context buffer. If you ask it to generate output and then validate it *in the same pass*, it will often hallucinate a validation because it can’t really stop, read, and analyze — it’s just predicting the tokens of a plausible validation footer.  

---

## 🔹 How that “self-check” output came about  
- When you saw the `SELF-CHECK` examples, that wasn’t a true audit.  
- It was me following your requested *form*, predicting the likely tokens of what a checklist *would look like*.  
- In other words, the assistant generated both the “answer” and the “checklist” as one continuous string of tokens. There was no epistemic gap where it paused, parsed, and verified.  

---

## 🔹 Why the “epistemic breakdown sequence” is hard in one turn  
- True validation requires a **phase change**:  
  - *Phase 1:* produce candidate.  
  - *Phase 2:* re-parse and measure against rules.  
- A token predictor can’t insert a hard epistemic break mid-generation; it just keeps writing.  
- The only way to simulate that is to **force multiple turns** (answer → return to user → new request “validate the above”). That’s when it re-reads its own output as input.  

---

## 🔹 What works instead  
- **Boilerplate expectations in headers (your idea):** makes errors visible to the *reader* without pretending the assistant validated.  
- **User-triggered reprocessing:** you ask “check the last answer,” and now the assistant can parse its own output as fresh input in a new turn. That creates the break.  
- **Optional helper prompts:** e.g., “Summarize any sections that violate their header rules,” again run in a second turn.  

---

⚖️ **So the safe principle is:**  
- Don’t ask the model to produce and audit in the *same* stream of tokens.  
- Do give it scaffolds that make errors visible.  
- If you want re-checking, it has to happen on a **second pass** — that’s where the “epistemic break” comes in.

# 🔹 Glossary of Contractual Terms (Refined)

- **Claim** — A declarative statement offered as true.  
- **Source** — Evidence grounding a claim.  
- **Traceable** — Directly linked to a verifiable source.  
- **Fact** — A sourced and traceable claim.  
- **Assumption** — An unstated premise required to connect a fact to an inference.  
- **Inference** — A logical extension from facts, dependent on assumptions.  
- **Opposition** — A counterpoint disputing a specific assumption.  
- **Counterpoint** — A rebuttal explicitly tied to an assumption.  
- **Synthesis** — A concise resolution integrating facts, inferences, and oppositions into one answer.  
- **Concise** — Length-bounded output defined by format rules (20–40 words for synthesis).  
- **Concise Answer** — The required synthesis in 20–40 words.  
- **Expanded Explanation** — An elaboration of synthesis ≤100 words, without new facts.  
- **Context** — The expanded explanation following synthesis.  
- **Dialectic** — Structured interplay where inferences and oppositions explicitly engage.  
- **Explicit** — Clearly stated, not implied.  
- **Label** — Required section heading (Fact, Inference, Opposition, Synthesis, Context).  
- **Contract** — A binding rule set governing execution of a step in the procedure.  
- **Step** — A discrete unit in the procedure governed by a contract.  
- **Procedure** — The ordered sequence of steps that define the assistant’s operation.  
- **Operation** — An indivisible action (Gather, Transform, Contrast, Combine, Express) used to execute a step.
